# Faculty appointments and the record of scholarship

## Authors

- Amy Brand<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0002-4208-1000](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4208-1000)) †

### Affiliations

1. is Assistant Provost for Faculty Appointments and Information at Harvard University where she manages the review of faculty appointments University-wide. Her career spans academia, publishing and scholarly communication technologies. She was program manager of the Harvard Office for Scholarly Communication from 2008 to 2009, and before that held long-term positions as an executive editor at the MIT Press, and as director of business and product development at CrossRef. She is also on the board of directors for ORCID. amy_brand@harvard.edu

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

Academic review committees would benefit from more details about the contributions made by individual researchers to papers with multiple authors, and also from more information about other types of scholarly communication.

## The importance of peers

It would be imprudent to generalize about Harvard's criteria for the appointment and promotion of faculty since the policies and procedures of the different Schools within the University all differ to a degree. And as Richard Zare, former chair of the chemistry department at Stanford University, described in a recent article (Zare, 2012), elite research institutions in the United States, seemingly unlike most of the world's universities, are not overly dependent on citation-based measures of impact such as impact factors for journals or h-indices for individuals. Rather, their appointment processes are time-intensive, more qualitative than quantitative or formulaic, and rely most heavily on peer review (both internal and external) to identify excellence. This type of peer review involves collecting confidential letters from a well-chosen set of peers: the purpose of these letters is to help academic review committees assemble a robust qualitative picture of a scholar's originality, independence, intellectual leadership and potential for future productivity and impact.

In 2010, Nature carried out a survey in which it asked readers about the use of metrics in decisions about new hires and tenure (Abbott et al., 2010). Three-quarters of the 150 readers who replied thought that metrics were being used in hiring decisions. However, provosts and other administrators contacted by Nature painted a different picture: ‘Metrics are not used a great deal,’ said Alex Halliday, head of the mathematical, physical and life sciences division at Oxford University. ‘The most important things are the letters, the interview and the CV, and our opinions of the papers published.’ Claude Canizares, vice president for research and associate provost at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, had a similar message: ‘We pay very little attention, almost zero, to citation indices and counting numbers of publications’.

While the letters that inform faculty appointments usually succeed in bringing the key considerations to light, I believe we could make the work of search and review committees easier and more reliable if we enhanced our sources of information about scholarship and contribution in ways that I describe below.We could make the work of search and review committees easier and more reliable if we enhanced our sources of information about scholarship and contribution.

## A broader record of scholarship

When a scholar's portfolio includes works outside of the published record of books, journal articles and conference proceedings, search and review committees often have to dig deeper to gauge the academic impact of those works. In the visual arts, for example, they may consult exhibition histories and published critiques, in addition to external reviews from a wider set of peers that might include curators and fellow artists. In the sciences, a candidate may have contributed meaningfully to his or her field by making data or software code widely available. In such cases, there is no choice at present but to rely on peer testimony to weigh the significance of the contribution.

Researchers and review committees alike would benefit greatly from the development of standards for the identification and citation of an extended set of scholarly works including data, software and code, multimedia and internet communications, so that such contributions are more readily integrated into our evolving digital scholarly ecosystem. ## Contributorship versus authorship

For the purposes of academic review, the traditional publication list is especially problematic when it comes to scholars with many multi-authored works. This is because author lists don't provide clear information about who contributed what in large-scale research and writing collaborations, which are increasingly common in the physical and life sciences. Author lists take a complex network of collaboration and effectively reduce it to a one-dimensional information source, where all we have to go by is order of names to convey author role and rank. Different fields of scholarship have adopted different practices around author order, but middle authors are always at the greatest risk of losing out on attribution and credit because their perceived contribution is diminished relative to first and last authors in collaborative works. In fields that list author names in journal articles alphabetically, such as economics, it has even been observed that you are more likely to get tenured in a top department if your surname begins with a letter earlier in the alphabet (Einav and Yariv, 2006). The unintended consequences of our authorship practices are far from benign for researchers and for science.

There is growing interest among researchers, funding agencies, academic institutions, editors and publishers in increasing the transparency of research contributions, and in more fine-grained tracking of attribution and associated credit. Many publishers now require contribution disclosures upon article submission—some in structured form, some in free-text form. There is now a clear need for a standard vocabulary of contributor roles that captures what each named author contributed to a particular publication—for example, conceptual framework, methodological design, data collection, data curation, experimental procedures, programming, software, statistical analysis, investigation, instrumentation, writing, illustration, project management, funding, laboratory head and so on. With the development of contributor role vocabularies and tagging mechanisms, the review committee of the future reading a tenure application from, say, a biostatistician who is usually a middle author in multi-authored works, will more readily be able to detect that the individual consistently contributes innovative methodologies to his or her research collaborations (IWCSA, 2012).

Imagine how the academic appointment process might change if search and review committees had access—within an appropriately tagged or linked online CV, for example, or via the ORCID system—to information about the specific contributions made by a candidate to each of his/her works, including contributions that might not otherwise have qualified for ‘authorship’ status? While a future scheme of standardized contributor roles integrated with the ORCID identifier system may lead to the development of new quantitative metrics, I am much more interested in having more precise information about researcher contribution made transparent in our information resources. On-going developments in academic publishing, along with the semantic capabilities of the web, should make this possible before too long.

results.result: Elite U.S. research institutions, including Harvard, use qualitative peer review processes rather than quantitative citation metrics for faculty appointments. These processes involve collecting confidential letters from peers to assess originality, independence, intellectual leadership, and future potential, though specific procedures vary across institutions.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C1-C4 are consistently supported by the author's institutional knowledge as Assistant Provost for Faculty Appointments at Harvard and citation to Zare (2012). The author's professional position provides credible firsthand knowledge of these practices, and the claims are internally consistent in describing a qualitative, peer-review-based system.

results.result: There is a disconnect between researcher perceptions and administrative reality regarding the use of metrics in faculty hiring. While three-quarters of Nature survey respondents believed metrics were used in hiring decisions, administrators at elite institutions (Oxford, MIT) reported minimal reliance on citation indices and publication counts, emphasizing instead letters, interviews, CVs, and qualitative assessment of papers.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C5-C8 are supported by citation to the Nature survey (Abbott et al., 2010) with specific data and direct quotes from named administrators at Oxford and MIT. The contrast between researcher perception (C5) and administrative testimony (C6-C8) is clearly documented with attributable sources, though the survey sample size (150 respondents) is relatively small and may not be representative.

results.result: Current faculty review processes face challenges in evaluating non-traditional scholarly outputs such as exhibitions in visual arts or data/software contributions in sciences. Review committees must rely on peer testimony and dig deeper to assess impact when works fall outside traditional publication formats, as standardized evaluation methods for these contributions do not yet exist.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C10-C13 are supported by the author's institutional knowledge and provide specific, concrete examples from different disciplines (visual arts, sciences). The claims logically connect the problem (difficulty evaluating non-traditional outputs) with current practice (reliance on peer testimony), and the examples are consistent with known practices in these fields.

results.result: Traditional author lists inadequately represent individual contributions in multi-authored works, which are increasingly common in physical and life sciences. Author order conventions vary by field but consistently disadvantage middle authors, with empirical evidence showing that in fields using alphabetical ordering (e.g., economics), earlier alphabet surnames correlate with higher tenure rates at top departments. These authorship practices have significant negative consequences for researchers and science.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C17-C24 form a coherent argument supported by citation to empirical data (Einav and Yariv, 2006) demonstrating the alphabet effect on tenure (C23). The logical progression from problem identification (C17-C20) through disciplinary variation (C21) to specific harms (C22-C24) is well-structured. However, C22's claim that middle authors are 'always' at greatest risk is overstated and not empirically validated across all fields.

results.result: There is growing stakeholder interest in improving transparency of research contributions and attribution tracking. Many publishers now require contribution disclosures (in various formats), creating a clear need for standardized contributor role vocabularies that can capture diverse types of contributions to publications.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C25-C28 are supported by the author's knowledge of trends in scholarly communication, consistent with observable developments in publishing practices. The progression from general interest (C25-C26) to current practices (C27) to identified needs (C28) is logical. However, the claims lack quantitative evidence for 'growing interest' or 'many publishers,' relying instead on general knowledge assertions.

results.result: The ORCID initiative was recently launched to provide every researcher with a unique identifier linked to their academic outputs and activities.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C15-C16 accurately describe ORCID's purpose and timing based on verifiable information about the initiative. The manuscript includes a figure showing the author's own ORCID page, providing direct evidence of the system's existence and functionality at the time of writing.

results.result: Enhanced information systems for tracking scholarly contributions and contributor roles could improve faculty review processes. While current peer review letters usually succeed in identifying key considerations, review committees would benefit from standardized systems providing detailed contribution information, broader scholarly output tracking, and integration with identifier systems like ORCID. Such developments are technologically feasible and could transform academic appointment processes.
results.result_reasoning: Claims C9, C14, C29-C32, C34-C35 are primarily speculative about future benefits and possibilities, marked as SPECULATION or INFERENCE in evidence types. While C33 acknowledges current systems work 'usually,' the proposed improvements lack empirical validation or pilot data demonstrating actual benefits. The claims represent reasoned proposals rather than demonstrated results, and C29's citation to IWCSA (2012) is not sufficient to validate the speculative future scenario described.
